summary:
EBK® – Rotation Compass is an agricultural decision-support prototype designed to help farmers make more informed crop-rotation decisions. The project focuses on Iowa, using county-level geographic data and historical NASA weather data to establish a foundation for location-aware agricultural insights.

We developed a web-based frontend and a FastAPI backend that work together to provide county information, farm data, local conditions, strategy endpoints, and forecast functionality. The platform is designed to bring relevant agricultural information into one accessible interface, supporting better-informed planning rather than relying solely on intuition or generalized recommendations.

This project is important because crop-rotation planning is closely connected to local environmental conditions and long-term agricultural sustainability. By combining geographic and weather data in a digital decision-support platform, EBK® aims to make agricultural planning more accessible, informed, and data-driven.
details:
Project Development and Technical Approach – EBK® Rotation Compass

EBK® – Rotation Compass was developed as a web-based agricultural technology solution, with an emphasis on turning different sources of agricultural and environmental data into a practical digital tool.

The application uses a modular architecture. On the client side, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript provide the interactive interface. On the server side, Python and FastAPI handle API requests and connect the application to its underlying datasets. The platform includes functionality for retrieving Iowa county information, accessing demonstration farm data, querying environmental conditions, and interacting with strategy and forecast endpoints.

An important part of the development was working with real datasets, particularly NASA historical weather data and county-level geographic information. This required consideration of data organization, accessibility, and the relationship between geographical locations and environmental conditions.

The project also involved practical software engineering decisions. We used Git and GitHub for source-code management, Render to host the backend, and Netlify to deploy the frontend. Separating these components allows each part to be maintained and developed independently.

What makes the project creative is the combination of environmental datasets, geographical context, and an accessible web interface in an agricultural application. Instead of treating weather and geographic information as isolated datasets, the project creates a framework through which they can contribute to agricultural decision-making.

Throughout development, we considered scalability, usability, data reliability, geographical relevance, maintainability, and deployment constraints. These considerations helped shape a foundation that can be extended with more sophisticated analytical capabilities in future development.
